These one hundred and eighty great nāga kings,
acting as leaders, together with other nāgas,
occasionally cause this great earth to tremble and resound.
Sometimes they emit light, and at other times they send down rain to ripen the crops.
When they come to see the Buddha, they receive the three refuges and the precepts.
They are freed from the fear of garuḍas, the fear of fiery sand, and the fear of royal affairs.
He shall always sustain the great earth and dwell in a palace of great jewels,
possessing long life, great majesty, wealth, and sovereignty;
with a vast circle of friends and followers, he will be able to crush his enemies.
Possessing great supernormal power and endowed with great radiance,
his form and color are perfect and his fame is widespread;
when the devas and asuras engage in battle, he manifests great majestic power.
All the sons, grandsons, brothers,
generals, ministers, and various envoys of those dragon kings likewise [rely] upon the Peacock King of Spells.
Protect me and my retinue for a lifespan of a hundred years;
yet, whether my retinue’s bodies are pure or impure through contact,
and whether they are intoxicated or sober, [protect us].
Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, going, or coming, may you be protected at all times.

Or when you are seized by devas, nāgas, asuras, mahoragas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, skandhas, unmādas, cetas, apasmārakas, uṣṭrakas, nakṣatras, or lipis—when you are thus seized or captured by such beings as these.
Protect me, [Name], along with all my retinue. Furthermore,
there are various spirits who consume vital essence, those who consume the fetus,
those who consume blood, and those who consume flesh.
Those who eat fat and grease, those who eat marrow,
those who eat limbs and joints, those who eat the raw,
those who eat life-force, and those who eat sacrificial offerings.
Those who feed on air, those who feed on fragrance,
those who feed on garlands, those who feed on flowers,
those who feed on fruits, and those who feed on the five grains.
Those who eat fire, those who eat pus,
those who eat excrement, those who eat urine,
those who eat saliva, and those who eat phlegm.
Those who eat mucus, those who eat leftover food,
those who eat vomit, those who eat impure things,
and those who drink leaking water.
When I, [Name], and my retinue are troubled and disturbed by such evil spirits and ghosts,
may this King of Peacock Mantras protect us all.
May they be freed from sorrow and suffering, live for a hundred years,
see a hundred autumns, and always experience peace and happiness.
Furthermore, if there are those who practice various malevolent sorcery or demonic enchantments...
They perform rites of exorcism and incantations,

fly through the air, and employ the *kṛtyā-karman* (sorcery), *kākhorda*, *gulma*, *piśāca*, *vetāla*, *vetāḍa*, and *piśācaka* to drink blood and marrow, transform people, and drive them into servitude.
They summon ghosts and spirits to create various evil karmas,
such as causing food to turn into vomit, casting evil shadows or evil glances,
producing malevolent talismans and scripts, or performing improper rites of transference for the dead.
When such various evils as these appear,
may they all protect me, [Name], and cause me to be free from sorrow and suffering.
Furthermore, regarding all matters of alarm and fear:
Fear of kings, thieves, water, fire, and the arrival of enemy armies;
fear of famine and fear of untimely death;
fear of earthquakes and fear of the approach of wild beasts.
May all such fears as those of evil associates and the fear at the time of death protect me,
[Name]. Furthermore, may all diseases— scabies, leprosy, sores, and ringworm— be likewise protected against.
Hemorrhoids, fistulas, carbuncles, and abscesses; the skin of the body becomes black and rough;
headaches and partial facial pain; indigestion;
and afflictions of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, mouth, lips, and teeth.
The throat, chest, back, flanks, waist, abdomen, thighs, calves,
hands, feet, limbs, joints, and private parts;
as well as mental distress, abdominal tumors, and the wasting diseases of emaciation and consumption.
All ailments and sufferings throughout the body shall be entirely eliminated.
Furthermore, malarial fevers occurring every one day,
two days, three days, four days, or even up to seven days [shall be cured].
Whether for half a month, a full month, or even on successive days;
whether for a brief moment or as a chronic fever;
or in cases of partial paralysis, goiters, or violent fevers caused by malevolent spirits.
Whether it be diseases caused by wind, heat, phlegm, or their combined accumulation;
or being possessed by spirits; or being afflicted by various poisons;
or being harmed by humans or non-humans.
When such evils and various diseases arise,
may they all protect me, [Name], as well as my kinsmen and dependents;
I now perform the binding of the boundary and the consecration of the ground for their sake.
By reciting and upholding this mantra, may all be rendered peaceful and secure. Svāhā.
And he spoke a verse, saying:
"May I be secure at night, and likewise during the day."
At all times, may the Buddhas always protect and keep me in mind. Homage to the Sugatas, the Buddhas. Homage to the Sugatas, the Bodhisattvas.

Devas, asuras, yakṣas, and others who have come to hear the Dharma, you should listen with a sincere mind; protect the Buddha-Dharma so that it may endure forever, and each of you should diligently practice the teachings of the World-Honored One. All disciples who have come here, whether dwelling upon the earth or in the sky, should always give rise to a heart of compassion toward humanity. Day and night, let yourselves abide according to the Dharma. May all worlds be ever peaceful and secure; may boundless merit and wisdom benefit all living beings. May all karmic offenses and hindrances be completely eliminated; may one distance oneself from all suffering and return to perfect stillness (*parinirvāṇa*). May the fragrance of the precepts be constantly used to anoint and polish the body; may the robes of meditative concentration always be worn to sustain the person.

Adorned everywhere with the wondrous flowers of Bodhi, wherever one dwells, may there be constant peace and happiness. *The Great Peacock King Spell Sūtra*, Scroll Middle. *The Great Peacock King Spell Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Lower.
The Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree,
translated this *Peacock King Spell* of Ānanda, which was joyfully proclaimed by the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:

*Tadyathā | a-ra-ti-ke-tu-ti-ma-te-ma-da-bha-da-ni-ava-re-savare-du-ri-du-ri-bu-ri-bu-ri-savare-paṇa-savare-hu-ṣṭhu-hu-ṣṭhu-hu-ṣṭhi-hu-ṣṭhi-mu-ṣṭhi-mu-ṣṭhi-svāhā*. Ānanda, this is the Great Peacock King of Mantras.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śikhin rejoiced in this and proclaimed it,

*Tadyathā | jñe jñe | kule kule | hili hili | mili mili | kidrumo | le | amale ambare avati | tambe tutambe | hili hili | guji guji | muji muji svāhā.* Ānanda, this is the King of Peacock Mantras.

Tadyathā | tatare tatare tatare | taradutare | vire viśaye | viśadare | arase arase | virase | viraja-male matic-maline | malini-siddhe | mantre śrīmantre śūri śūri śūri śūri | vadaravati-siddhe svāhā. Ānanda, this is the Peacock King Mantra.

Tadyathā | hiri hiri | kiri miri | iri lirī kṣatari | kidumuri | aṭa pāri | dhakhe dhatte dhaṅkhe buruke busade | narukante kamani | kambudaluki | taru taru varali prakkṛti | ḍaṃṣṭre | mīle tatre | idihase | aṭṭale | dūbale bhogile | bhaṭi bhaṭi | kevaṭi bhaṭi | caṭa daṃbe | aṭa daṃbe | up to this point, according to one’s desired aim.
All must be recited as previously explained in detail.
When praying for rain, one should say:
"May the heavens send down rain, pervading the ten directions and universally moistening all things."

Just as he rescued the bhikṣu Śāriputra from the peril of snake venom,
so too is this now-proclaimed Peacock King of Mantras;
it shall cause all sentient beings who read and recite it, uphold it, or transcribe it [to attain liberation].
All shall attain peace and happiness;
their aspirations shall be fulfilled as extensively described before,
even unto themselves and their retinues living for a hundred years.
Furthermore, Ānanda, this Great Peacock King of Mantras was joyfully proclaimed by the Bodhisattva Maitreya for the benefit of sentient beings.
He then spoke the mantra as follows:

Tadyathā | Śrī śrī śrībhadre | Sthiti sthiti sthitibhadre | Hrīḥ hrīḥ hrīḥ hrīṇi danti śaphale | Śikhaśūlabhani | Buddhi buddhi buddhi | Buddhisattvaṃ hi buddhiparicāriṇi svāhā | Ānanda, this is the Great Peacock Spell-King (*Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī*).
The Brahmā Sahāmpati, Lord of this Sahā World,
joyfully proclaimed it and spoke this mantra:

*Tadyathā | hiri hiri | miri miri | marīci paṅkuli | kili kili | kili kili | kili kili varāha-maṇḍa-kuṇḍake ṭake ṭake vimaha vimaha puse | dara dara | hara hara | hara hara | puru puru | puru puru | svāhā* This mantra can eliminate evil poisons and extinguish evil poisons.
The power of the Buddha removes poison; the power of the Pratyekabuddha removes poison;
the power of the Arhat removes poison; the power of the noble ones on the three fruits and four stages of approach removes poison;
and the power of those who speak truth removes poison.
The power of the staff of Brahmā; the power of Śakra’s vajra;
the power of Vaiśravaṇa’s flying wheel and the power of his conflagration;
and the power of the nāga kings’ noose.
The illusory power of the asuras, the electric power of the nāga kings,
the power of the tridents of Huluhudala,
and the power of the spears of Skandha.
By the power of the Great Peacock Mantra-King,
may all poisons be eliminated and made to enter the earth.
May I, [Name], and all my retinue attain peace and security.
Furthermore, there are the poisons of various nāgas, the poisons of malevolent spirits and enchantments,
the poisons of humans and non-humans,
the poisons of bites from teeth, and the poisons of thunderstorms, venomous snakes, and rats.
The poisons of bees, flies, centipedes, and frogs;
the poisons of scabies, leprosy, carbuncles, abscesses, fistulas, and boils;
the poisons of medicine, incantations, humans, and non-humans.
May all such poisons as these be utterly extinguished.
May the poison and suffering of myself, [Name], and my retinue be entirely removed and dispersed, sinking into the earth. Svāhā.

punished by Śakra,
and punished by the ṛṣis.

Punar-gandharva!

or punished by water and fire.
In all places, whatever punishments and minor disciplinary measures there may be.
May all [beings] be far removed from me, [Name],
as well as from all my retinue.
One will always see protection,
live for a hundred years,
and witness a hundred autumns, Ānanda; you should receive and uphold the names of all these thirty-five kings of rivers.
If one knows this, then at all places—
when crossing rivers, streams, seas, or marshes— one will encounter no calamities or difficulties.

and the King of the Vakṣu River.

Answer: To the King of the Bhadra River,

From Lake Anavatapta, the four great rivers—

and so forth— flow out into Jambudvīpa.
And there are the various river-deity kings belonging to the other rivers such as the Yangtze,
Yellow, Huai, and Ji, who dwell depending upon this great earth,
possessing diverse forms and diverse colors.
They accomplish the vidyā-mantras that manifest bodies according to one's wishes and perform auspicious or inauspicious deeds.
All these deities, together with their retinues,
likewise rely upon this Great Peacock King of Mantras.
Protect me, [Name], along with all my retinue;
may we live for a hundred years, free from all sorrow and affliction. Svāhā!

Mount Cakravāḍa, King of Mountains;

There is King Indraśaila,
King Brahmavihāra,
and King Śrīparvata.

and Mount Māramanohara-kuśala-rāja.

and Satyaratnaśailendrarāja.

the King of Mountains, Suvarṇakūṭa.

and Mount Subāhu.

Dundubhi Śailarāja,
and Suśīma Śailarāja.

Mount Jñānaśuddha-rāja,
and Mount Kandaraka-rāja.
Mount King Wondrous Garlands,
Mount King Sword-Shaped,

"May you always behold auspiciousness and be free from all sorrow and affliction, svāhā!

Kīṭarājabuddha-gambhīrabuddhi-pate!

The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, together with the twenty-eight yakṣa generals, all recited this Great Peacock Mantra-King; the great yakṣa general Pāñcika, Hārītī with her five hundred sons, and all their retinues likewise rejoiced in it.
Furthermore, Ānanda, it is said of this Great Peacock Spell-King: this Great Peacock Spell-King must not be transgressed and must not be treated with contempt.

Whether they be devas, nāgas, asuras, mahoragas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, skandhas, unmādās, cetas, apasmārās, or śitavaktras—none of these gods and spirits can transgress this Peacock Spell-King.
Furthermore, there are all those malevolent spirits and ghosts—
namely, those who consume vital essence, those who consume the fetus, those who consume blood, those who consume flesh,
those who consume fat and grease, and those who consume marrow.
Those who eat limbs and joints, those who eat the raw,
those who eat life-force, those who eat sacrifices,
those who eat breath, and those who eat fragrance.
Those who eat garlands, those who eat flowers,
those who eat fruits, those who eat the five grains,
those who eat what is burnt by fire, and those who eat pus.
Those who eat excrement, those who eat urine,
those who eat saliva, those who eat drool,
those who eat nasal mucus, and those who eat leftover food.
Those who eat vomit, those who eat impure things,
those who eat leaking water—
such are the various types of evil eaters.
Furthermore, they cannot transgress this King of Peacock Mantras.
Moreover, there may be those who employ various malevolent spirits,
curses, incantations, and sorcery to fly through the air.
Kṛtyakarmāṇaka-kuṭṭhaka-irṣyā-dharṣaṇa-vitarda-attada-vitada-cittaja-pilīsakā;
they drink blood and marrow, transform into humans, and drive them into servitude.
They summon ghosts and spirits to create various evil karmas;
they cause food to turn into vomit through evil gaze and evil shadows;
they produce malevolent talismans and scripts, or perform wicked rites of transference for the dead.
When such various evils appear, may they all protect me,
[Name], and cause me to be free from sorrow and suffering.
Furthermore, regarding all matters of alarm and fear:
Fear of kings, thieves, water, fire, and the arrival of enemy armies;
fear of famine, fear of untimely death,
fear of earthquakes, and fear of the approach of wild beasts.
May such fears as those of evil associates and the fear at the time of death all protect me,
[Name]. Furthermore, may all diseases— scabies, leprosy, sores, and ringworm— be likewise protected against.
Hemorrhoids, fistulas, carbuncles, and abscesses; the skin of the body becomes black and rough;
headaches, partial facial pain, and indigestion;
[afflictions of] the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, mouth, lips, and teeth.
The throat, chest, back, flanks, waist, abdomen, thighs, calves,
hands, feet, limbs, joints, and private parts;
as well as mental distress, vertigo, chronic ailments, emaciation, and wasting diseases.
All ailments and sufferings throughout the body shall be completely eliminated.
Furthermore, regarding malarial fevers occurring every day,
every two days, every three days, every four days, or even every seven days—
Whether for half a month, one day, or even on successive days;
whether for a brief moment or as a chronic fever;
or in cases of partial paralysis, goiters, or the high fevers caused by malevolent spirits.
Whether it be diseases caused by wind, heat, phlegm, or their combined convergence;
or being possessed by spirits, or afflicted by various poisons;
or being harmed by humans or non-humans.
When such evils and various diseases arise,
if one recites this Great Peacock King Spell,
it shall not fail to fulfill whatever is sought according to one's wishes.
May you all protect me, [Name], along with my retinue.
I now establish a boundary and consecrate the ground for their sake;
by reciting and upholding this mantra, may they all be made secure and at peace. Svāhā.
And he spoke this verse:
"May I be secure by night, and likewise during the day;
at all times, may the Buddhas always protect and mind me."
Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be anyone who invokes the name of this Great Peacock King of Spells to protect others or to protect themselves, [they shall be shielded].
Or one may tie a cord or thread and wear it upon the body; by doing so,
if that person should deserve the death penalty, they shall be released through the payment of a fine,
and if they should deserve a light flogging, they shall be released through [the payment of] a fine.
One who deserves a light flogging shall be released after being reviled;
one who deserves reviling and reprimand shall be released after being reviled and reprimanded;
one who deserves reprimand shall be released naturally.
All illnesses and sufferings will completely dissipate;
none shall dare to transgress [this power].
This person shall also have no fear of kings, thieves, water, or fire.
Though harmed by malicious weapons or staves,
one shall sleep and wake in peace and always see auspicious dreams;
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one shall encounter no adversity or harm and attain an extended lifespan.
Except for those karmic actions performed in previous lives that result in a short lifespan,
or those that must be experienced as the primary retribution (vipāka),
Ānanda, whether it be at a time of flooding or a time of great drought.
If one recites this Great Peacock King Spell, all the nāgas will rejoice;
if it rains, the sky will immediately clear, and if there is drought, rain will fall.
Whether it be men or women, whatever their aspirations may be, they shall swiftly attain fulfillment. Ānanda, this is the Great Peacock King Spell.
Merely by recollecting it, one is able to eliminate all fears, diseases, and anxieties;
how much more so by fully reading, reciting, and upholding it!
You should receive and uphold this Great Peacock King Mantra.
Desiring to benefit and protect the fourfold assembly—
the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās— and to free them from all fears,
he further spoke this mantra:
Greed, hatred, and delusion—these are the three poisons of the world;
the Buddha has completely severed them.
By his words of truth, he eliminates greed, hatred, and delusion—these three poisons of the world.
The Dharma has already severed [the poisons]; by true speech, poison is extinguished.
Greed, hatred, and delusion—these three poisons of the world—the Saṅgha has already severed; by true speech, poison is eliminated.
All the World-Honored Ones possess great majestic power;
these Arhats of renowned fame remove poison and bring peace and security.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, [acted accordingly].
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him three times to the right, he took his leave of the Buddha and departed.
He went to where the bhikṣu Śāriputra was;
upon arrival, he immediately [recited] this Peacock Spell-King.
I shall provide protection for that bhikṣu;
by binding the boundary and consecrating the ground, I will sustain and benefit him, removing his suffering and distress.
Thus, the bhikṣu Svāti attained peace of body, his poisonous afflictions dissipated, and he rose from the ground.
He then went together with the Venerable Ānanda to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet,
and having reported all these matters in detail to the World-Honored One, stood to one side.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "By this cause and condition,
you should communicate this Great Peacock King Spell to those of the seven classes—
bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās— as well as to kings, ministers, and others."
Exhort them to single-mindedly receive, uphold, read, and recite [this scripture],
ensuring they master it thoroughly so that they may explain it to others and clarify its meaning.
Copy the scriptural volumes and circulate them wherever possible, making offerings of incense, flowers, food, and drink according to one's means.
May all sentient beings be forever free from sorrow and suffering and always experience peace and happiness.
May they attain immeasurable merit that is inconceivable.
When these words had been spoken, at that time—
Ānanda and the great assembly—
devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, maruts, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
Having heard all that the Buddha has taught, they were all greatly rejoiced, and with faith and acceptance, they put it into practice.
May the devas, asuras, yakṣas, and others who have come to hear the Dharma, with sincere hearts,
protect and uphold the Buddha-Dharma so that it may endure forever, and may each of them diligently carry out the teachings of the World-Honored One.
All you disciples who have come here, whether dwelling upon the earth or abiding in the sky,
may you always give rise to a heart of compassion for the human world; may you abide in accordance with the Dharma throughout day and night,
and may all worlds be forever peaceful and secure, benefiting all living beings through boundless merit and wisdom.
All karmic obscurations are completely eliminated; Free from all suffering, one returns to parinirvāṇa.

Constantly anointing the body with the fragrance of ethical discipline, Always wearing the robes of meditative concentration to sustain the self, Adorned everywhere with the exquisite flowers of bodhi— Wherever one dwells, there is constant peace and happiness.
The Sūtra on the Great Peacock Spell-King Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Two: Next, the ritual methods for painting images at the maṇḍala site are explained.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"If there are men or women..."
Whatever they pray for— whether it be great rain or a great drought,
calamities, warfare, various diseases, pestilence,
or any other such undesirable matters.
Those who wish to recite this Great Peacock King Spell (Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī) in the hope of its power to eliminate [afflictions] should perform the ritual in this manner:
having leveled the ground in a secluded place, they should proceed as follows.
One should construct a small mandala-platform, four or five finger-widths high and three or four cubits square;
it may sometimes be larger.
One should take fresh cow dung that has not fallen to the ground and smear it cleanly upon the platform.
Within this maṇḍala, install an image of the Buddha facing west.
To the left of the image, place an image of Mahāmāyūrī;
whether sculpted or painted, it should be adorned according to the ritual rules.
Alternatively, one may erect three or four peacock feathers upon a clean brick pedestal and likewise smear it with cow dung;
by performing any one of these three acts, the purpose is achieved.

Use white *avakā* flowers—which are not found in this region and may be substituted by pear blossoms (*nālikera*) or the like—or white *karavīra* flowers, which are found south of the [Himalayan] ridges but not in the north and may be substituted by white apricot, crabapple, or *śatapatrī* (Chinese hibiscus) blossoms; or use *śirīṣa* tree flowers—which is the *nyagrodha* tree—or *bimbi* tree leaves, which are also not found in this region and may be substituted by jujube, mulberry, or lotus leaves, scattered upon the altar.
First, before the Buddha, one should provide various foods and drinks as they are available, making all manner of offerings.
Next, before the Bodhisattva Mahāmāyūrīrāja, one should do the same.
Having wholeheartedly offered a dish of honey-water, sugar-water, cow’s milk, curd, cakes, and rice,
hold a censer in your hand and burn agalloch incense.
Facing east, perform the offerings as previously requested.
Invoke the Buddha, the assembly of noble ones, and the host of the Four Heavenly Kings by calling each of their names individually with a sincere heart.
"Come to protect me, [Name], and all my retinue,
so that we may all attain peace and security and live for a hundred years.
Next, at the eastern side of the altar:
Offer a plate of candied sugar cakes, milk porridge,
and rice with candied sugar syrup to the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his retinue of gandharvas.
Next, at the southern side of the altar:
Place a gruel of sesame oil and a bottle of *si-du* water, along with a plate of cakes and rice,
as an offering to the deity Kubera and his retinue,
the Guardian Kings of the North. Next, on the western side of the altar, place a gruel of milk and a bottle of milk, along with a plate of cakes and rice.
Offerings are made to the deity Virūpākṣa, the King of the Heavenly Kings, and the various nāgas and other spirits.
Next, on the northern side of the altar,
place a bowl of rice mixed with curd, a bottle of sidhu liquor, and a dish of cakes and rice.
One should make offerings to the divine beings such as the Yakṣas and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa;
furthermore, according to the season, one should arrange various flowers and fruits,
and burn aloeswood incense, storax, and frankincense as a universal offering.
The patient suffering from the epidemic should sit peacefully on the right side of the Buddha,
facing west, while the mantra-reciter faces east;
one or two peacock feathers may then be taken.
Alternatively, one may brush the body of the sick person with *kuśa* grass,
reciting the aforementioned Heart Mantra twenty-one times while calling the sick person's name; having performed this offering three times each day, morning, noon, and evening.
Place all the offered food in water,
or bury it in the ground so that it cannot be eaten and is not stepped upon.
Thoroughly wipe the entire mandala site with mud.
Alternatively, one may smear the ground with cow dung;
this is the standard ritual method for making offerings to the Peacock King.
Whatever one seeks, one may construct this altar according to the Dharma.
If one is poor and has nothing, one should provide offerings according to what is currently available.
Next, the method for painting an image is explained:
take a new white cotton cloth.
The pigments should be mixed with wood glue, not animal hide glue.
Place them in a new cup.
The person who paints the image should do so at dawn.
Having bathed for purification and put on new clothes, one should receive the eight precepts.
Thereafter, one should fashion an image of the Buddha;
it should be made of gold.
Wearing a saffron-colored robe,
he sits upon a golden lion throne;
to his left, paint the deity Mahāmāyūrī.
Reddish-white in color, she wears a white skirt and a white upper garment with a white cord draped over her shoulders.
Her body has four arms, and all her ornaments are made of gold.
She stands upon a lotus flower or upon a golden throne.
In his right hands, one holds a *yuzu* (citron) and the other grasps a lotus flower. In his left hands,
one holds an auspicious fruit (*śrīphala*) as large as a melon, yellowish-red in color— a species not found in this region— and the other grasps three stalks of peacock feathers.
Between the Buddha and the Bodhisattva, paint an image of the Golden Peacock King standing upon a jewel-adorned lotus flower;
before his throat, draw the figure of a *svastika* using ox-gall.
To the side of the Buddha, depict the noble Ānanda kneeling with palms joined;
in the space between them, depict the divine king Vajrapāṇi,
holding a white fly-whisk in his right hand and grasping a vajra-trident in his left.
On all four sides of the Buddha, paint various flowers and fruits as offerings.
On the eastern side, paint the shape of the continent of Pūrvavideha like a half-moon;
within it, paint the Gandharva Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with his retinue.
Surrounded by the gandharva deities, one should paint Jambudvīpa on the southern side of the Buddha;
it is shaped like a chariot, broad in the north and narrow in the south.
In its center, one should paint Pāñcika, the Guardian King Virūḍhaka.
Surrounded by a multitude of Kumbhāṇḍa spirits,
one should depict the continent of Aparagoyānī in the shape of a full moon on the western side of the Buddha;
within it, one should depict the Nāga King Viśāla-netra.
Surrounded on all sides by hosts of nāgas,
one should paint Uttarakuru in the north of the Buddha; it is square in shape,
and within it, one should paint the yakṣa king Vaiśravaṇa.
Surrounded by various yakṣa deities,
once the image has been painted, it is installed within the maṇḍala;
as before, one exits facing west.
On the first day of the waxing moon, one should extensively arrange offerings before the painted image.
One should recite the heart-mantra or other mantras from within the sutras.
Next, one should have a pure young girl spin the thread.
Before the painted image, one should recite the mantra while tying knots until one hundred and eight knots are made.
The practitioner should tie [the cord] behind their own elbow;
this is the method for protecting the body. One's companions and assistants should likewise employ this protective rite.
When one wishes to perform the ritual, one must first cultivate the preliminary preparations.
One should recite this mantra ten thousand or one hundred thousand times:
*Namo bhagavate amale vimale siddhiṃ me [name] and my retinue*.
On the fifteenth day, before the painted image,
take yellow ox dung and construct another square altar measuring four cubits on each side.
Upon that altar, arrange white non-glutinous rice to form the shapes of the four continents.
In each of those locations, one should arrange offerings as previously described.

In the west, burn ghee mixed with agallochum incense;

As before, perform these offerings before the Buddha and the deity Mahāmāyūrī.
They burned various kinds of famous incense and extensively presented offerings of diverse foods and drinks, as well as various flowers and fruits.
Furthermore, they used gold, silver, copper, tin, and iron.
Form them into five pills, each like the pit of a jujube seed.
Place them upon seven layers of bodhi leaves—or, if these are unavailable, substitute with mulberry leaves—and set them before the image.
Next, dig into the ground in front of the altar to construct a fire hearth.
In a square space one cubit wide and one foot deep, kindle a fire so that it burns steadily.
Next, use *udumbara* wood and *pālaśa* wood—which are not found in this region and may be substituted with mulberry or jujube wood—as well as the stalks of *gojihvā* grass.
From one of the three [types of wood],
cut pieces five inches long and as thick as a finger;
eight hundred such pieces are required for each recitation of the mantra.
Recite the mantra once and cast it into the fire along with ghee and mustard seeds.
If there is the howling of a *śiva* in that direction, it is the cry of a jackal; as previously described, one should arrange the offerings for that direction accordingly.
All companions should likewise not be afraid;

this is the sign of the accomplishment of the mantra. If there are no auspicious signs and the matter is not accomplished, take five pellets from the leaf and recite the mantra over them eight hundred times.
Immediately, all matters will be accomplished according to one's wishes.
One takes a golden ball and places it in one's own mouth,
while a companion gives one to them as they please.
In all cases, there is no need to swallow it; one should simply remove it from wherever it is found.
If there are other people present, one may take a portion from the food offering about the size of a jujube fruit and have each of them eat it.
To eliminate all illnesses and fulfill whatever one seeks according to one's wishes, there is another method: one should go to a place where corpses are disposed of,
or toward a crossroads,
and perform the aforementioned altar ritual without installing a painted image.
Simply arrange offerings of food and drink, incense, flowers, and other articles for the deities of the four directions to provide mutual protection;
furthermore, perform the rite of burning incense in the hearth and reciting mantras over colored threads.
If one attains the *kāryakaraṇa-svairī* (the state of acting according to one's will),
one will see auspicious dreams at night, such as dreaming of fine chariots and excellent oxen or elephants,
or seeing high mountains and fruit-bearing trees.
Alternatively, one may see oneself ascending to a lofty hall or a magnificent palace,
and behold one's parents as well as other noble persons;
one may also see oneself wearing upper garments and encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Or one may see young girls, boys, and girls,
adorned with exquisite ornaments, seated upon fine beds and mattresses,
amidst various flowers, fruits, and auspicious objects.
Some see celestial deities reporting the actual facts;
some see milk, curd, various crops, raw meat, and fresh fish;
or they see fine horses, peacocks, and the like.
These are all signs of auspiciousness;
if they differ from these, they are not favorable omens—
for instance, if one dreams of donkeys, mules, or camels.
Monkeys, pigs, dogs, snakes, scorpions, cats, and mice;
owls, crows, eagles, and vultures—naked and without refuge;
as well as foul vessels, dry firewood, and empty huts.
Cemeteries, thickets, and rivers will dry up.
The Vināyakas are obstructive deities with elephant heads and human bodies; people in the western regions mostly make offerings to these, all of whom are inauspicious signs.
Whenever one performs any rite of incantation,

This applies even in all places of terror.
Or, at times of all kinds of illness and suffering,

calamities, and untimely deaths shall be entirely dispelled.
If a child falls ill or is possessed by a spirit, one should brush them with a peacock’s tail while reciting the mantra; they will immediately be freed from suffering.
Alternatively, by binding them with a consecrated cord, they shall all receive healing and recovery.
If other mantra rituals for constructing maṇḍalas have not reached completion, by performing this Peacock King rite,

As the World-Honored One has said:
even if a person has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution,

Alternatively, by stabilizing the mind, one can eliminate various illnesses; this is based on the fundamental intent.
With pure faith, all matters will be accomplished, whereas for those lacking faith, they will not.
Ānanda, there is furthermore a heart-mantra which you should receive and uphold.
The mantra is as follows:

*Namo buddhāya | namo dharmāya | namaḥ saṃghāya | namo suvarṇaprabhāsottama-mayūrarājāya | namo mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñyai || Tadyathā | ajite jaye | vajre khadhe khecare khagarbhe akṣaye mokṣe | irimele girimele | hurulave mahāhurulave | padmagarbhe | timiṅgile mahāṅgule svāhā ||* Ānanda, this is the heart-mantra of Mahāmāyūrī.
This is what has been proclaimed by all the Buddhas; this is the concise dharma.
Those who wish to receive, uphold, read, or recite it should perform all the ritual procedures for the maṇḍala as previously described.
Whatever aspirations one may have shall all be fulfilled.
If a matter does not accord with one's wishes,

If, while reciting the mantra before a painted image,

If one sees a woman approaching, this is what is sought.
Such distinctions arise through the compassionate response of the devas.
If there is faith and a desire to constantly uphold [this practice] and seek protection, [one shall succeed].
One should paint this Bodhisattva deity Mahāmāyūrī.
As before, place a peacock in front of her image and install it in a clean place within the room, constantly making offerings to it.
All fears, all sufferings of illness, and all undesirable events shall be entirely eliminated.

If one wishes to uphold this practice and seek accomplishment, one should begin the ritual on the first day of the waxing moon and construct the maṇḍala; it must not be performed during the summer months, for otherwise the rite will not succeed.

having bathed for purification and donned fresh, clean garments,

Recite the mantra from the aforementioned sūtra or the heart-mantra seven times;
having completed this, speak these words:

Please come to receive these incense, flowers, and various foods and drinks.

As previously mentioned, one may invoke by name all the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, and all other spirits.

Then the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms, received [the teaching] upon his head,
